tagline: Battlefield earthworks, river cliffs and the former resort at Seven Springs
intro: North Carolina’s transportation department lists the Blue-Gray Scenic Byway among its Coastal Plain routes. The department says its byways offer an alternative to the traffic and commercial areas of major highways and interstates.

At Bentonville, the landscape preserves evidence of a different kind of passage: earthworks built by Union and Confederate forces. The battle took place March 19–21, 1865; the Harper House served as a Union field hospital. The house survives, while its kitchen and enslaved people’s quarters are reconstructions.
Near Seven Springs, the Cliffs of the Neuse rise 90 feet above the river. Seven Springs itself lies beside the Neuse, while Trenton is the seat of Jones County.

moments.title: Bentonville Battlefield
moments.text: The Harper House is the only building surviving from the time of the Battle of Bentonville. It served as a field hospital for the Union’s Fourteenth Army Corps during the battle of March 19–21, 1865. The restored house is accompanied by a reconstructed kitchen and enslaved people’s quarters, a distinction that matters when reading the site. Beyond the buildings, earthworks made by both armies remain visible. Outdoor exhibits include the Federal XX Corps reserve trenches, the Harper family cemetery and a Confederate cemetery. Walking trails follow original trenches built during the battle.
moments.notice: Earthworks built by Union and Confederate forces remain visible in the battlefield landscape.

moments.title: Cliffs of the Neuse
moments.text: Sand, clay, seashells, shale and gravel make up the colored face of the Cliffs of the Neuse. The cliffs extend for 600 yards and rise 90 feet above the water. Their story begins with a shift in the Earth’s crust: the river followed a fault line and cut through sediments left by shallow seas. A bend brought the water against the bank, where erosion carved the cliffs. In 1944, landowner Lionel Weil proposed preserving the area; land donations helped establish the state park the following year. The exposed layers range from white and tan to yellow and brown.
moments.notice: The cliff face has layers of white, tan, yellow and brown.

moments.title: Seven Springs
moments.text: Seven Springs carried two versions of another name before adopting the one on today’s map. Incorporated as Whitehall in 1855, it was reincorporated as White Hall in 1881. That same year, a hotel and resort opened to draw visitors to seven nearby mineral springs. The resort closed in 1944, and the town became Seven Springs in 1951. Its position beside the Neuse also brought destructive flooding: Hurricane Floyd in 1999 halved the population. Hurricanes Matthew and Florence brought further decline; the 2020 census counted 55 residents. The population had peaked at 207 residents in 1960.
